lead: Today's readings ask what will remain when everything is shaken. Hebrews promises “a kingdom that cannot be shaken” and calls us to thank God for it. In Luke, a sincere ruler asks the way to eternal life, and finds that his wealth holds him more tightly than he knew. Peter's reply, “we have left our homes and followed you”, receives a promise. The key words are unshaken and follow.

r.h: A kingdom that cannot be shaken
set: These verses close the comparison between Sinai and Zion that began in 12:18. At Sinai God spoke on earth and the earth shook (Exodus 19:18). Now he speaks from heaven through his Son. Hebrews quotes the prophet Haggai, who promised after the exile that God would shake heaven and earth and fill his house with glory (Haggai 2:6–7).
str: v. 25: do not refuse the one who speaks from heaven.
vv. 26–27: the final shaking, which removes what is made and leaves what cannot be shaken.
vv. 28–29: so give thanks and worship with reverence, for God is a consuming fire.
kw: Used of the kingdom we are “receiving”. The present tense matters: the kingdom is being given now, and we are receiving it.
Literally “let us have grace” or “gratitude”. Thanksgiving is the right answer to a gift. The Greek word for thanksgiving, eucharistia, became the name of the Church's great act of worship.
vv: See that you do not refuse the one who is speaking;
God is still speaking. The danger is not that he is silent but that we turn away.
This phrase, “Yet once more,” indicates the removal of what is shaken … so that what cannot be shaken may remain.
Everything made will be tested. What remains is what belongs to God's kingdom.
for indeed our God is a consuming fire.
Words from Deuteronomy 4:24. The fire that frightened Israel at Sinai is the same holy love that purifies and does not destroy what is true.
ch: The Church hears in verse 28 a description of the Holy Qurbono, the thanksgiving in which we receive the kingdom and offer “acceptable worship with reverence and awe”. The Catechism teaches that the Eucharist is above all thanksgiving to the Father (CCC 1359–1360). The fire of verse 29 is not something to run from. In the Syriac tradition the Holy Mysteries themselves are often called fire, which those who come in faith and reverence receive without harm.

set: Luke places this meeting on Jesus' long journey to Jerusalem. Just before it, Jesus has blessed the little children and said that the kingdom must be received like a child (18:15–17). Only Luke calls the questioner a “ruler”, perhaps a leader in a synagogue or a man of standing. Matthew says he was young (Matthew 19:20). Mark adds that Jesus looked at him and loved him (Mark 10:21).
str: vv. 18–21: the question and the commandments.
vv. 22–23: “one thing lacking”; the ruler's sorrow.
vv. 24–27: the camel and the needle; what is possible for God.
vv. 28–30: Peter's word and Jesus' promise.
kw: A man with position as well as money. What he must leave is not only property but status.

The largest animal in the land and the smallest opening anyone could picture. The saying is a deliberate exaggeration. There is no good evidence for the popular story of a small gate in Jerusalem called “the needle's eye”.
Peter's words, translated “our homes” in the NRSV. The disciples had left their own boats, nets and families.
vv: Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?

A good question asked sincerely. Jesus' reply, “No one is good but God alone”, is not a denial of his own goodness. It directs the man to the source of all goodness, the God who now stands before him.
There is still one thing lacking. Sell all that you own and distribute the money to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come, follow me.
The point of the command is the last words: “follow me”. The poor gain, and he gains treasure, but the real gift offered is Jesus himself.
What is impossible for mortals is possible for God.
Salvation is never a human achievement. Even letting go of what we cling to is a grace.
Then Peter said, “Look, we have left our homes and followed you.”
Peter is not boasting; he speaks for all who have left something for Jesus. The Lord's answer promises much more in this age and eternal life in the next.
ch: The Catechism uses this meeting to teach that the commandments are the first step on the way to eternal life, and that following Jesus is their fulfilment (CCC 2052–2053). The Church has never read the passage as a condemnation of all property. It calls every Christian to detachment, so that riches serve love of God and neighbour (CCC 2544–2547). Clement of Alexandria wrote a whole treatise, Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved?, to show that what must be given up is the soul's attachment to wealth (in substance).

rite: The Panchangam remembers today St Cletus, also called Anacletus, Bishop of Rome. St Irenaeus names him as the successor of Linus, to whom the apostles Peter and Paul had entrusted the Church of Rome (Against Heresies III.3.3). Very little else is known of him. His memory reminds us that the faith reaches us through an unbroken line of shepherds, and that the Church of Rome, with which our Church is in full communion since 1930, has kept the apostles' teaching from the first generation.
study: What in my life do I hold so tightly that I would be sad if Jesus asked me to let it go?
Hebrews calls us to give thanks for an unshakable kingdom. For what will I thank God at the next Holy Qurbono?
